description: Maker operations: what the bot is quoting, what it decided, and whether its inputs are alive. Rows top to bottom answer, in order: is it quoting near fair value and is it alive; what did each tick decide and under which regime; how is inventory tracking; and are the feeds healthy. One market at a time via the selector, except the heartbeat, feed-health, and tick-error panels, which are process-wide by design. Every table here is written by the maker bot fire-and-forget: a gap can mean the bot stopped OR that its writes are failing, and only the container logs separate those two.

panels.description: The composed fair value against the book actually resting on-chain, with takes overlaid. Read the gap, not the levels: `fair value` vs `reference (on-chain)` is the drift the trigger policy is tolerating, and `reference (candidate)` is where this tick would move it. A `best bid`/`best ask` that stops while fair value continues usually means that side went dark (a freeze-side, a halt, or a book killed for staleness) — the series ends rather than dropping to zero, which is why nulls are never spanned here. But check the tick-outcome band before concluding it: a tick whose vault read failed also breaks these series, and there a full ladder may still be resting and matchable. Dark and unknown look identical on this panel; `TickError` below is what separates them. Fills are scaled out of the indexer's raw atoms ratio; see the panel query.

targets.rawSql:
SELECT
  to_timestamp(ts) AS "time",
  fair AS "fair value",
  on_chain_reference AS "reference (on-chain)",
  reference AS "reference (candidate)",
  best_bid AS "best bid",
  best_ask AS "best ask"
FROM maker_telemetry
WHERE $__unixEpochFilter(ts)
  AND market = ${market:sqlstring}
ORDER BY ts

WITH market AS (
  SELECT
    market_pubkey,
    power(10::numeric, base_decimals - quote_decimals) AS price_scale
  FROM maker_telemetry
  WHERE market = ${market:sqlstring}
  ORDER BY ts DESC
  LIMIT 1
)
SELECT
  to_timestamp(t.block_time) AS "time",
  (t.avg_price * m.price_scale)::double precision AS "fill"
FROM takes t
JOIN market m ON t.market = m.market_pubkey
WHERE $__unixEpochFilter(t.block_time)
ORDER BY t.block_time

panels.title: Quotes vs fair value — $market

panels.description: Seconds since the newest telemetry sample across ALL markets — the bot's heartbeat. Not filtered by market on purpose: any market's sample proves the process is alive, so filtering would read one market's halt as a dead bot. Rising without bound means the maker is gone OR its database writes are failing; the two are indistinguishable from here, and `Feed health` plus the container logs are what separate them. Empty (`No data`) means no sample has ever been written.

targets.rawSql:
SELECT
  (extract(epoch FROM now()) - max(ts))::bigint AS "seconds since last sample"
FROM maker_telemetry

panels.title: Heartbeat

panels.description:
The estimator's own defensibility: the number the system believes, drawn over the prints it was built from, with each source's share of that number on the right axis.

This is not the panel above. "Quotes vs fair value" asks whether our QUOTES track our fair; this asks whether the FAIR is defensible against its inputs. Read them in that order during an incident.

PRICE ARMS (left axis). Three series per selected market — the composed fair price, the FX leg's fused estimate, and the FX leg's fast consensus median — against every selected source's raw ticks. Read the GAPS, which is why all three are drawn. Fused-vs-fast is the estimator's whole contribution: they sit on top of each other while the sources agree, and separate exactly when one source is being ignored or a dislocation is being adopted. Fused-vs-scatter shows the estimator declining to chase a stray print.

WEIGHT ARMS (right axis, dashed step, 0 to 1). Each source's share of its leg's fused estimate, per tick — which names what the price arms only imply. A series pinned at ZERO is the interesting case, not an empty one: zero means the source answered and was TRIMMED, sitting outside the dispersion band of the fast consensus, so the estimator declined to believe it. That is a sick feed, a mis-mapped product, or a genuine disagreement between an official reference rate and the tape, and it is exactly what must not be averaged away silently. A source that stopped answering has no row at all and leaves a GAP instead. Shares over one leg-tick sum to exactly 1 on a seeding or re-seeding tick — trimming does not change that, because a trimmed source contributes no precision and so takes nothing out of the total. Only an ordinary update leaves them summing to less than 1, and that shortfall is the prior estimate's own share, deliberately not drawn because no feed is accountable for it.

TWO WAYS THIS PANEL IS EMPTY, and they are different facts. If the Market picker itself is empty, NO MAKER HAS EVER WRITTEN to this database — the picker is driven from maker telemetry, so it has nothing to offer, and the Heartbeat panel above reads dead for the same reason. That is a bring-up state, not an error, and nothing you select will fix it. Only if a market IS selected and the fair line still draws over an empty scatter is this a picker pairing: a market's symbol (EURC) and its FX product id (EUR-USD) are different vocabularies with no join in the schema, so the Source and Product pickers cannot be correlated for you.

targets.rawSql:
-- The estimator's output over its raw inputs. Each arm is a bare
-- column inside the epoch-filter macro: Grafana captures a macro
-- argument with a regex that stops at the first closing paren, so a
-- to_timestamp(...) call inside one truncates the argument and the
-- query fails to interpolate. The conversion happens in the SELECT
-- list, never in the macro.
--
-- Raw prints: the scatter the fused line is judged against.
SELECT
  to_timestamp(observed_at) AS "time",
  source || ' ' || product_id || ' tick' AS metric,
  price AS value
FROM spot_ticks
WHERE $__unixEpochFilter(observed_at)
  AND source = ANY (ARRAY[${source:sqlstring}]::text[])
  AND product_id = ANY (ARRAY[${product_id:sqlstring}]::text[])
UNION ALL
-- The fair price: the composed mid the maker quotes off, which is now
-- built from the fused leg estimates rather than the bare medians.
-- NULL exactly when the composition paused, and left as a gap rather
-- than zero-filled -- a paused market and a market worth nothing are
-- different facts.
SELECT
  to_timestamp(ts) AS "time",
  market || ' fair (fused)' AS metric,
  fair AS value
FROM maker_telemetry
WHERE $__unixEpochFilter(ts)
  AND market = ANY (ARRAY[${market:sqlstring}]::text[])
  AND fair IS NOT NULL
UNION ALL
-- The FX leg's two numbers, which is where the estimator is actually
-- visible: `fused_value` is what the composition priced off and
-- `value` is the fast median that guards dislocations.
SELECT
  to_timestamp(ts) AS "time",
  market || ' fx estimate (fused)' AS metric,
  fused_value AS value
FROM maker_legs
WHERE $__unixEpochFilter(ts)
  AND market = ANY (ARRAY[${market:sqlstring}]::text[])
  AND leg = 'fx'
  AND fused_value IS NOT NULL
UNION ALL
SELECT
  to_timestamp(ts) AS "time",
  market || ' fx consensus (fast)' AS metric,
  value
FROM maker_legs
WHERE $__unixEpochFilter(ts)
  AND market = ANY (ARRAY[${market:sqlstring}]::text[])
  AND leg = 'fx'
ORDER BY 1

-- Per-source fusion weights. Deliberately NOT filtered to weight > 0:
-- a zero-weight row is a source that answered and was trimmed, which
-- is the single most useful thing this table records. Filtering it out
-- would leave a fused estimate with no record of what it refused.
--
-- The mechanism filter IS required, though, and for the opposite reason.
-- The table is keyed by mechanism so the resolver's consensus attribution
-- can land additively; those weights are exact linear-combination shares
-- rather than shares of posterior information. Omitting this predicate
-- would plot two vocabularies on one axis and double every series the
-- day they arrive.
SELECT
  to_timestamp(ts) AS "time",
  market || ' ' || leg || ' ' || source || ' weight' AS metric,
  weight AS value
FROM maker_leg_contributions
WHERE $__unixEpochFilter(ts)
  AND mechanism = 'fusion'
  AND market = ANY (ARRAY[${market:sqlstring}]::text[])
ORDER BY 1

panels.title: Fair price over its sources

panels.description: What each tick decided, including the outcomes that end the tick early. `Quote` is normal; `Reshape` and `FreezeSide` are the graduated de-risking steps; `Halt` is a kill switch; `Pause` means no usable reference; `Frozen` means the vault is frozen on-chain; `TickError` means the tick failed before deciding anything (see the errors table below); `Unknown` should never appear and means a code path reached no outcome. Note that `TickError` and a decision are not exclusive — a tick that decided `Halt` and then failed to send it shows `Halt` here, with the failure in the errors table, so count failures by `tick_error IS NOT NULL` rather than by this band. Every one of these is written by the bot on its way out of the tick, so a gap here is an absent bot rather than an idle one — or a sample dropped under telemetry backpressure, which is visible only in the bot's log, since delivery here is at-most-once.

targets.rawSql:
SELECT
  to_timestamp(ts) AS "time",
  action AS "tick outcome"
FROM maker_telemetry
WHERE $__unixEpochFilter(ts)
  AND market = ${market:sqlstring}
ORDER BY ts

panels.title: Tick outcome — $market

panels.description: Which regime priced this market and the health gate the kill switches ran under. Health is a total function of the regime, so exactly six pairs are reachable and all six are mapped here — an unmapped pair would fall through to the base style and read as healthy. `Normal / Ok` is FX x basis with both legs live. `CryptoOnly` is structural over the FX weekend, not a fault. Anything `Degraded` tightens every kill-switch threshold. `Paused / Pause` means no usable leg at all. The two `Unverified` states are permanent and deliberately not treated as degraded: `FxPinned` has no basis source to observe, and `Uncorroborated` prices off a single unchecked source — the standing condition for most of the roster, which is why it is distinguished from `Normal / Ok` rather than sharing it.

targets.rawSql:
SELECT
  to_timestamp(ts) AS "time",
  regime || ' / ' || health AS "composition"
FROM maker_telemetry
WHERE $__unixEpochFilter(ts)
  AND market = ${market:sqlstring}
ORDER BY ts

panels.title: Composition regime / health — $market

panels.description: The vault's two legs valued in USD, their total, and the launch baseline the drawdown floor is measured against. The legs crossing is the inventory skew's whole input; TVL falling toward `launch TVL` scaled by the floor fraction is what trips the TVL kill switch. NULL (a gap) means the tick never valued the vault — a failed read, a frozen vault, or a paused composition — which is not the same as an empty vault.

targets.rawSql:
SELECT
  to_timestamp(ts) AS "time",
  base_value_usd AS "base leg (USD)",
  quote_value_usd AS "quote leg (USD)",
  tvl_usd AS "TVL (USD)",
  launch_tvl_usd AS "launch TVL (USD)"
FROM maker_telemetry
WHERE $__unixEpochFilter(ts)
  AND market = ${market:sqlstring}
ORDER BY ts

panels.title: Inventory — $market

panels.description: The inventory skew applied to the mid, in bps, signed. Its sign should track the inventory imbalance above: long the base leg skews the reference down to lean into offloading it. A skew pinned at a constant is the cap being hit.

targets.rawSql:
SELECT
  to_timestamp(ts) AS "time",
  skew_bps AS "reference skew (bps)"
FROM maker_telemetry
WHERE $__unixEpochFilter(ts)
  AND market = ${market:sqlstring}
ORDER BY ts

panels.title: Reference skew — $market

panels.description: Each leg's reading age, as the ENGINE aged it — which is not `now() - sample time`. The FX anchor is aged from the publisher's own clock (Pyth publishes a `publish_time`), so a reading received this tick can legitimately be minutes old, and over the FX weekend it ages without bound while the crypto-only regime carries the mid. That is the signal, not a bug. There is no per-venue series here any more: a leg is a candidate set resolved by consensus, so the age shown is the resolved reading's. Which sources backed it, and which one is the suspect when they disagreed, is the Leg consensus table below.

targets.rawSql:
SELECT
  to_timestamp(ts) AS "time",
  leg AS metric,
  age_secs AS value
FROM maker_legs
WHERE $__unixEpochFilter(ts)
  AND market = ${market:sqlstring}
ORDER BY ts

panels.title: Feed staleness — $market

panels.description: Published confidence half-width as a fraction of the reading, for the legs whose source publishes one (Pyth Hermes does; a plain REST quote does not, and contributes no series here). Widening past the engine's bound puts the market in the fresh-but-uncertain regime, which widens the spread rather than stopping quoting — so a rise here is expected to show up as a wider touch above, not as a halt.

targets.rawSql:
SELECT
  to_timestamp(ts) AS "time",
  leg AS metric,
  confidence / value AS "confidence (fraction of value)"
FROM maker_legs
WHERE $__unixEpochFilter(ts)
  AND market = ${market:sqlstring}
  AND confidence IS NOT NULL
  AND value > 0
ORDER BY ts

panels.title: Feed confidence — $market

panels.description: Every registered feed source's current liveness, written by the framework's metrics seam rather than by any per-feed wiring — so a venue adapter added later appears here on its first poll with no change to this dashboard. Not filtered by market: a source is shared across the roster. `ok_age_secs` is measured off `last_ok_at` alone, which is the point of tracking it separately from `last_error_at` — a feed erroring on every retry would look fresh by a single `updated_at`. A row with status `ok` and a populated `last_error` has RECOVERED; the error text is kept deliberately so a flap remains diagnosable after the fact.

targets.rawSql:
SELECT
  feed,
  status,
  coalesce(extract(epoch FROM now()) - last_ok_at, 9999999)::bigint AS ok_age_secs,
  to_timestamp(last_ok_at) AS last_ok,
  caught_up,
  last_records,
  ok_count,
  error_count,
  to_timestamp(last_error_at) AS last_error_at,
  last_error,
  to_timestamp(updated_at) AS last_seen
FROM feed_health
ORDER BY status ASC, feed

panels.title: Feed health (all sources)

panels.description:
How each leg's sources resolved, latest per market and leg. This is what replaced per-venue attribution: a leg is a candidate set, so there is no single answering feed to name.

Read `consensus_state` first. `Corroborated` (3+ agreeing) and `Agreed` (2 agreeing) are healthy. `SingleTrusted` is one source designated believable alone. `SingleUnverified` is one source with nothing corroborating it — for most of this roster that is the STEADY STATE, not a fault, and it is the only signal that a market is quoted off one unchecked feed; a market appearing here that the coverage survey did not predict is a genuine signal. `Dispersed` means the sources disagreed beyond the band, and then `dispersion_outlier` names the source furthest from the consensus — the SUSPECT to distrust, never 'the feed that answered'.

A leg missing from this table usually resolved to nothing: either no source offered a reading, or every candidate was too stale. But it can also mean the row was dropped — legs and their sample are separate records sharing one timestamp, and delivery is at-most-once, so under backpressure a sample can land with its legs lost. Confirm against the bot's log before reading a gap as a resolution failure. Which source went quiet is the feed-health table, which is per source rather than per leg.

targets.rawSql:
SELECT
  market,
  leg,
  consensus_state,
  contributor_count,
  dispersion_outlier,
  round(age_secs::numeric, 1) AS age_secs,
  fresh,
  to_timestamp(ts) AS observed
FROM (
  SELECT DISTINCT ON (market, leg) *
  FROM maker_legs
  WHERE ts > extract(epoch FROM now()) - 3600
  ORDER BY market, leg, ts DESC
) latest
ORDER BY market, leg

panels.title: Leg consensus (all markets)

panels.description: The most recent ticks that failed outright, newest first, across every market. These are the ticks that reached no decision at all — typically a vault read timing out — and they are recorded rather than dropped precisely so that a stalled maker is distinguishable from a quiet one. Empty is the healthy state.

targets.rawSql:
SELECT
  to_timestamp(ts) AS "time",
  market,
  action,
  tick_error
FROM maker_telemetry
WHERE $__unixEpochFilter(ts)
  AND tick_error IS NOT NULL
ORDER BY ts DESC
LIMIT 100

panels.title: Recent tick errors (all markets)

panels.description: Transport state for push sources, which the feed-health table above deliberately does not cover. A push source's records arrive only when its venue has something to send, so no age on this row means anything: a link that has been up for a week with no fills is healthy, and there is intentionally no staleness column here to read otherwise. What to look at is `state`, and then `connects` — a count that has climbed while the state reads `up` is a link that keeps dropping and re-establishing, which is the failure that most resembles a working one. `last_error` is retained across a recovery, so read it with `last_error_at`.

targets.rawSql:
SELECT
  feed,
  state,
  to_timestamp(last_up_at) AS last_up,
  to_timestamp(last_down_at) AS last_down,
  connects,
  disconnects,
  to_timestamp(last_error_at) AS last_error_at,
  last_error
FROM push_health
ORDER BY state ASC, feed

panels.title: Push feed transport liveness

list.definition: SELECT DISTINCT market FROM maker_telemetry WHERE ts > extract(epoch FROM now()) - 86400 ORDER BY 1
list.description: The market to inspect. Single-select: the per-market panels overlay several series each, so stacking the roster on top of that would be unreadable. Lists only markets the bot has actually written a sample for, so an empty selector means no telemetry has arrived at all rather than a bad default.
list.label: Market
list.name: market
list.query: SELECT DISTINCT market FROM maker_telemetry WHERE ts > extract(epoch FROM now()) - 86400 ORDER BY 1

list.definition: SELECT DISTINCT asset_class FROM instruments ORDER BY 1
list.description: Asset class, from the instruments dimension - the class a pair's two legs imply rather than a label anyone maintains, so re-seeding a currency's kind reclassifies every pair using it with nothing to backfill. Queried rather than hardcoded for the same reason the Product picker is: a fixed list is wrong the moment the roster changes, and wrong silently. Expect an 'unclassified' bucket to be selectable - the dimension left-joins deliberately so a pair whose leg is not yet seeded stays visible rather than vanishing from every class filter, which would hide its data while the panel still rendered.
list.label: Class
list.name: class
list.query: SELECT DISTINCT asset_class FROM instruments ORDER BY 1

list.definition: SELECT product_id FROM instruments WHERE asset_class = ANY (ARRAY[${class:sqlstring}]::text[]) ORDER BY 1
list.description: Every product any collector is configured to poll, from the instruments dimension, narrowed to the selected Class. Registry-driven rather than a scan of the measurement tables, which matters three ways: it covers both tiers by construction - most of the roster is tick-only, since only EURC reaches a CEX candle endpoint - a newly added pair appears before its first row lands, and it costs one small-table read instead of a DISTINCT over two unbounded tables on every dashboard load. The class filter uses the sqlstring formatter inside an ARRAY, not a regex inside a quoted literal: the regex formatter does not escape quotes, and ARRAY[] stays valid SQL when nothing is selected where IN () is a syntax error. Defaults to the three MVP FX pairs rather than All, and that default is load-bearing rather than taste: the OHLC panel repeats over this variable at full width, so All renders one full-width chart per instrument. At 33 instruments that is 33 stacked charts pushing roughly 330 grid rows between the top of the dashboard and everything under it - including Tick coverage and Source coverage, which are the only two panels where a tick-only venue such as Kraken appears at all. Most of those charts are also empty, since the default candle source carries candles for a single product. Drill-down is unaffected: the drop-down still offers every product and All.
list.label: Product
list.name: product_id
list.query: SELECT product_id FROM instruments WHERE asset_class = ANY (ARRAY[${class:sqlstring}]::text[]) ORDER BY 1

list.definition: SELECT DISTINCT source FROM instrument_registry ORDER BY 1
list.description: Sources from both tiers, so the tick-only venues (kraken, pyth, erapi, frankfurter) are selectable rather than absent. Note that 'coinbase' appears once but writes both tiers - the table a row lives in is what distinguishes a print from a bucket, not the source label.
list.label: Source
list.name: source
list.query: SELECT DISTINCT source FROM instrument_registry ORDER BY 1

title: Maker operations
